extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists), especially those writing fantasy and science fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for novelists on designing and describing fictional worlds and settings—covering worldbuilding, setting description, environmental detail, and using setting to support character and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative and vivid description
rubrics_metrics.description: Good novel settings require imaginative and vivid description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immerse your readers in a mesmerizing fictional world so they will want to turn the page, not close the book. Use sensory detail and striking images to make places memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting as time and place (backdrop)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is the time and place that forms the backdrop for your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete temporal and spatial anchors so readers understand where and when events occur; use setting to orient the reader without overwhelming them with exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to mirror characters' psychologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing how to describe setting vividly helps you craft settings that mirror your characters' psychologies and personalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose details of a character's home or environment that reveal who they are (e.g., cluttered rooms, sparse furnishings) and let setting illuminate inner states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of setting: time, place, mood, social and cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements of setting - time, place, mood, social and cultural context - help to make a novel feel real and alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all these ingredients when building a world; social and cultural context are as important as physical geography for believability and plot possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding questions to create a civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: World building is an important concept... Good world building questions will help you create a detailed and immersive world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use probing questions about institutions, history, technology, economy, religion, and daily life to flesh out believable societies and avoid shallow or inconsistent cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural environment shapes hazards and mood
rubrics_metrics.description: In epic fantasy world building, natural environments provide possible hazards (freezing cold, dangerous volcanoes) and mood or atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use environmental features to create conflict, set tone, and influence plot choices; even in realist fiction, environment details make settings feel familiar and lived-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to anchor action and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving readers a vivid sense of where and when events take place anchors action and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce place early in scenes so that movement and speech are grounded; use selective detail rather than encyclopedic description to keep pace and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid story setting description as functional (e.g., highlight turning points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivid story setting descriptions help anchor a story's action in place and can reveal varied functions of setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use setting description strategically—for example, to highlight character turning points or to contrast past and present—rather than as filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create immersive, interesting and believable settings regardless of genre
rubrics_metrics.description: It's important to create immersive, interesting and believable settings, whatever your genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply worldbuilding rigor even in non-fantastical genres: consistency, sensory detail, and plausible social structures increase reader immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce place effectively: setting the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting the scene: 6 ways to introduce place in stories — giving readers a vivid sense of where and when events take place anchors action and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methods for introducing place (brief anchors, sensory hooks, character interactions with environment) that suit the scene's pacing and tone; techniques apply to both fiction and nonfiction scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding as vehicle for social critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating fantasy worlds can be an excellent means for social critique because writers can imagine worlds entirely different from our own and highlight our quirks and issues through contrast and similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use invented institutions, norms, or contrasts between worlds to comment on real-world issues subtly; ensure critique arises naturally from the world rather than feeling didactic.
